title: Student Privacy & Campus Surveillance Security Checklist
metaDescription: Protect your student data and privacy rights with our comprehensive checklist covering campus surveillance, proctoring software, and educational privacy.
intro: As a student, your privacy rights are constantly challenged by campus surveillance systems, proctoring software, and edtech platforms. This checklist helps you understand and protect your educational privacy rights while navigating modern digital learning environments.

items.task: Learn your FERPA rights and protections
items.why: FERPA gives you control over your educational records and who can access them, but many students don't know their rights.
items.howTo: Visit your school's registrar office or website to get a copy of your FERPA rights. Understand that you can restrict directory information and control record access after age 18.

items.why: Schools often have broad data collection policies that students unknowingly agree to during enrollment.
items.howTo: Locate your school's privacy policy on their website. Pay attention to sections about data sharing, third-party services, and monitoring policies. Take notes on concerning practices.

items.task: Audit all consent forms you've signed
items.why: Many privacy waivers are buried in enrollment paperwork, giving schools extensive monitoring rights.
items.howTo: Contact the registrar's office to request copies of all consent forms you've signed. Review each for data collection and monitoring permissions you can revoke.

items.task: Opt out of directory information sharing
items.why: Schools can share basic info like name, address, and phone number unless you specifically opt out.
items.howTo: Submit a written request to your registrar to suppress directory information. This prevents sharing with military recruiters, employers, and marketing companies.

items.task: Identify third-party services with access to your data
items.why: Schools share student data with numerous vendors for services like email, learning management, and analytics.
items.howTo: Ask your IT department for a list of all third-party services that process student data. Research each company's privacy practices and data retention policies.

items.why: Understanding camera placement helps you make informed decisions about privacy in different campus areas.
items.howTo: Walk around campus and note camera locations, especially in study areas, dormitories, and common spaces. Check if your school publishes surveillance maps online.

items.why: Campus networks often monitor and log all internet activity, creating detailed profiles of student behavior.
items.howTo: Use a VPN like those recommended by privacy advocates when on campus Wi-Fi. Consider using a privacy-focused browser for sensitive browsing to limit tracking.

items.why: Student ID cards often contain RFID chips that track your location and activities across campus.
items.howTo: Ask campus security about ID card tracking capabilities. Consider using RFID-blocking wallets and understand which campus activities are logged via your ID.

items.why: Dorm rooms may have monitoring policies and RAs may have broad access rights that compromise privacy.
items.howTo: Review your housing contract for privacy clauses. Understand RA inspection rights, security camera policies in common areas, and internet monitoring in dorms.

items.task: Protect library and study space privacy
items.why: Libraries track computer usage, book checkouts, and study habits, creating detailed academic profiles.
items.howTo: Use library computers in private browsing mode, understand checkout record retention policies, and ask about study space surveillance practices.

items.why: Official campus apps often request excessive permissions for location, contacts, and device access.
items.howTo: Review permissions for all school-related apps on your phone. Disable location services, contact access, and microphone permissions unless absolutely necessary.

items.task: Research your school's proctoring software policies
items.why: Proctoring software can access your entire computer, record your environment, and store biometric data.
items.howTo: Request documentation about proctoring software data collection, storage, and sharing practices. Understand what data is recorded and how long it's retained.

items.why: Proctoring software records your room, potentially capturing private information about your living situation.
items.howTo: Create a dedicated testing space with minimal personal items visible. Use a neutral background and ensure no sensitive documents or information are in view.

items.why: Proctoring software may access files, applications, and data beyond what's necessary for the exam.
items.howTo: Use a separate user account or dedicated device for proctored exams. Close all unnecessary applications and temporarily move sensitive files to external storage.

items.why: Some proctoring software collects facial recognition data, keystroke patterns, and behavioral biometrics without clear consent.
items.howTo: Ask your institution about biometric data collection, storage duration, and deletion policies. Request opt-out options if available.

items.why: Students may have rights to alternative testing methods that don't require invasive monitoring.
items.howTo: Contact your disability services office or academic advisor about alternative testing arrangements. Some accommodations may allow in-person or less invasive testing.

items.why: School laptops and tablets often have comprehensive monitoring software that tracks all activity, even personal use.
items.howTo: Review the acceptable use policy for school devices. Ask IT about monitoring software installed and whether personal use is tracked and stored.

items.why: Using school devices for personal activities creates privacy risks and potential disciplinary issues.
items.howTo: Never use school devices for personal browsing, social media, or private communications. Use your own device and Consider a privacy-focused browser for additional privacy.

items.task: Configure Learning Management System privacy settings
items.why: LMS platforms often share more data than necessary and have privacy settings students can control.
items.howTo: Log into your LMS and explore privacy settings. Limit profile visibility, disable activity tracking where possible, and review what information is shared with instructors.

items.task: Request your data from educational technology platforms
items.why: EdTech companies collect extensive data about learning patterns, performance, and behavior that you have rights to access.
items.howTo: Contact major EdTech platforms your school uses to request copies of your data. Common platforms include Canvas, Blackboard, Pearson, and McGraw-Hill systems.

items.task: Audit school cloud storage and email privacy
items.why: School email and cloud storage are often monitored and may not have the same privacy protections as personal accounts.
items.howTo: Review policies for school email and cloud storage. Understand data retention, monitoring, and sharing practices. Use personal accounts for sensitive communications.

items.task: Plan for data cleanup after graduation
items.why: Schools may retain student data indefinitely unless you take action to limit retention and sharing.
items.howTo: Create a plan for data cleanup before graduation. Request deletion of unnecessary records, update contact preferences, and understand alumni data sharing policies.

pro_tips: Document everything: Keep records of all privacy-related communications with your school, including emails, forms, and policy documents for future reference.
Use the buddy system: Work with classmates to compare notes on privacy policies and share strategies for protecting data while meeting academic requirements.
Know your state laws: Some states have stronger student privacy protections than federal FERPA requirements - research your local student privacy rights.
Create a privacy-focused study setup: Use tools like a privacy-focused browser and VPNs consistently, and maintain separate devices or accounts for personal vs. academic use.
Stay informed about policy changes: Schools often update privacy policies mid-semester - set up alerts or regularly check for changes that might affect your rights.
